cloze.title: 原文选词填空
cloze.instruction: 从词库中选择合适的词填入空白，每词使用一次，保留原文词形。大小写不影响判分。

parts.text: But Britain’s breeding starling population has declined dramatically over recent decades, while changes in climate, migration and

are reshaping the lives of many birds. Could these wider changes also be affecting murmurations? By repeating a major citizen-science survey we carried out 12 years ago, we’re hoping to find out whether these spectacular displays are

in size, timing or location.

According to the British Trust for Ornithology, the UK’s breeding starling population declined by 61% between 1995 and 2024. This is part of a wider pattern of bird declines: the UK’s farmland bird population

has fallen by 62% since 1970, with intensification of farming playing a major role. But that doesn’t necessarily mean individual murmurations are becoming smaller. Changes in where birds gather, when they arrive and how they behave could all

the displays we see each winter.

Climate change may also be playing a part in shifting patterns and timings of murmuration displays. Britain’s winter starling population includes large numbers of birds arriving from continental Europe. As winter conditions change, so might their migration patterns,

affecting the timing, location and size of murmurations. Changes in food availability and roosting habitat could also be important.

Our original citizen-science project began in 2014. Working with the Royal Society of Biology, we
people power to record murmurations between 2014 and 2016. Volunteer citizen scientists submitted more than 3,000 observations, noting the size, duration and location of murmurations, plus the

of any birds of prey. Observations from 23 countries provided an unusually large dataset.

Back then, our main question wasn’t whether murmurations were changing, but why they happened at all. Over the last 20 years, scientists have made considerable

in understanding how thousands of birds coordinate their movements, with each responding to its neighbours to produce those extraordinary patterns. But why do starlings gather in such spectacular formations in the first place?

One explanation was that the displays helped

birds to communal roosts, where gathering in large numbers might provide warmth. Another was that murmurations helped protect starlings from predators such as peregrine falcons and sparrowhawks. Moving together in a dense, constantly changing
could make it harder for a predator to single out a specific bird, while providing more eyes to detect approaching danger.
